plan.contextChunk: This figure is a horizontal strip in which the same wireframe camera appears five times, evenly spaced across a white field and interleaved with thick red arrows. Each camera is a viewing frustum seen from behind and slightly below: a solid black dot at the bottom marks the projection center, four straight edges rise from it to the corners of a wide rectangle standing for the image plane, and lines cross that rectangle to its lower corners, so the pyramid reads as pointing up and away from the viewer. The five copies match exactly in size and orientation. Red arrows run horizontally along the base of the strip, one before the leftmost camera, one in each of the four gaps, and one trailing off the right edge, every arrowhead pointing right. Because the frusta aim away from the viewer while the arrows travel across the picture, the motion is perpendicular to the line of sight rather than along it. The sequence illustrates sideways camera motion parallel to the image plane, as when a scene slides past the side window of a moving car, in which the forward velocity component is zero.

elements: five identical wireframe camera frusta evenly spaced along a horizontal strip
black dot (projection center / camera origin) at the bottom of each frustum
wide rectangle representing the image plane at the top of each frustum
four straight frustum edges rising from the black dot to the rectangle corners
diagonal lines crossing each image-plane rectangle to its lower corners
six thick red arrows running along the base of the strip, all pointing right: one before the leftmost camera, one in each gap, one trailing off the right edge
in the optical-flow view: a projected image frame showing two scene points (one near, one far) with horizontal flow vectors

interactions.label: Slide camera sideways
interactions.teaches: Pure lateral translation moves the camera parallel to its image plane — the forward velocity component is zero, so the whole scene appears to slide sideways like a view from a car window

interactions.label: Lateral displacement
interactions.teaches: As the active camera translates from left to right, the induced shift of projected scene points grows proportionally — apparent image motion is linear in lateral displacement

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching to the projected flow view reveals that the near point's flow vector is longer than the far point's — lateral translation produces depth-dependent parallax in the image

demo_steps.title: Zero displacement
demo_steps.narration: The active camera sits at the first station; both scene points project to their reference positions and no flow is visible.

demo_steps.title: Translate sideways
demo_steps.narration: Slide the displacement to 2: the camera moves two stations right along the red-arrow path while its frustum keeps pointing forward — motion is perpendicular to the line of sight.

demo_steps.title: Flow at full displacement
demo_steps.narration: At displacement 4, switch to the optical-flow view: the near point's vector is clearly longer than the far point's, showing parallax inversely proportional to depth.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Strip spans X ∈ [-11, 11], all elements near Z = 0, camera strip height ~2.6 world units in Y. Five frusta centered at X = -8, -4, 0, +4, +8. Each frustum: black dot (sphere r≈0.18) at local (0, 0, 0); image-plane rectangle 2.0 wide × 1.2 tall standing vertically, centered ~1.9 units directly above the dot; four edges connect the dot to the rectangle corners; one diagonal cross line from each upper corner to the opposite lower corner of the rectangle. All five copies identical in size and orientation, image planes facing the viewer (frustum apex at bottom, opening up and slightly away). Six red arrows (#e01919, shaft thickness ~0.12, arrowhead length ~0.5) lie on the baseline y ≈ -0.4, each ~3.4 units long, pointing +X, occupying the left margin, the four gaps, and trailing off the right edge. Optical-flow view: a flat image frame ~3 × 2 units with two dots — near point (orange #ff8800, depth Z=2) and far point (blue #1a66cc, depth Z=6); flow vector magnitude = f·t/Z with f=1, so the near vector is exactly 3× the far vector for the same slider displacement t. Colors: frusta black lines on white, dots black, arrows red.
interactionPlan.notes: Draw frusta with THREE.LineSegments (EdgesGeometry-free: explicit line pairs) so the diagonal cross lines render exactly as in the source. For the animation, translate the active camera along +X over the five station positions while ghost outlines mark the stations; project the two scene points through the moving pinhole each frame. In the flow view, hide the strip and show the image frame with arrows sized by f·t/Z; keep both views in the scene and toggle visibility. Slider position can map continuously across the strip (not just station snaps) with the four ghost frusta fading in proportionally.

authoredContext:

the figure. This will happen if you are looking
through a side window of a car at the scene passing by. In this case,
the forward velocity is zero, $V_Z=0$.
